**One:** The doubled form means tearing down and demolishing, while the single form means they left them and abandoned them as ruins, empty. This was related by Ibn Jarir. **First:** Whenever the Muslims gained control over one of their houses, they demolished it to widen the space for fighting, while they themselves would breach their houses and go out into what lay beyond them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

**Second:** Whenever the Muslims demolished part of their fortresses, they tore down what they had built of what the Muslims had ruined. This was said by al-Dahhak.

As for these names: the mention of "Allah", "al-Rahman", and "al-Rahim" has already preceded in [al-Fatihah], and we have mentioned the meaning of ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ in [al-An'am: 73]. And ﴿al-Malik﴾ in surah [al-Mu'minun: 116].

As for "al-Quddus" (the Holy): Abu al-Ashhab, Abu Nuhayk, and Mu'adh al-Qari read it with a fatha on the qaf. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: "al-Quddus" is the one pure from defects, exalted above rivals and offspring. And "al-qudus" (holiness) is purity. From it is named Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House), and its meaning: the place in which one is purified from sins. It was said of Paradise: "hazirat al-qudus" (the enclosure of holiness), for its purity from the afflictions of this world. And "al-qudus" is the basin in which one purifies oneself. Among names, none of the form fu''ul with a damma on the first letter has come except "Quddus" and "Subbuh"; and it may also be said: Quddus and Subbuh with a fatha on both, which is the analogical form for names, as in their saying: safud and kalub.

As for "al-Salam" (the Peace): Ibn Qutaybah said: He named Himself Salam for His being safe from what befalls creation of defect, deficiency, and perishing. Al-Khattabi said: its meaning is: the Possessor of peace. And "al-Salam" in the attribute of Allah, glorified is He, is the One who is free from every defect, and clear of every calamity and deficiency that befalls created beings. He said: it has been said that He is the one from whose injustice creation is safe.

As for "al-Mu'min", there are six sayings concerning it.

The first: that He is the one from whose injustice people are safe, and from whose punishment those who believe in Him are safe. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil.

The second: that He is the Protector (al-mujir), said by al-Qurazi.

(p-226) The third: the one who confirms the believers when they affirm His oneness, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that He is the one who affirmed His own oneness, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. Mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: that He is the one who fulfills His promise to His servants, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The sixth: that He confirms the assumptions of His believing servants and does not disappoint their hopes, like the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, related from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic: "I am as My servant thinks of Me." Related by al-Khattabi.

As for "al-Muhaymin", there are four sayings concerning it.

The first: that He is the Witness, said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Kisa'i. Al-Khattabi said: from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and a witness over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], so Allah is the Witness over His creation by what occurs from them of speech or action.

The second: that He is the Trustworthy (al-Amin), said by al-Dahhak. Al-Khattabi said: its origin is mu'ayman, then the hamza was changed to a haa, because the haa is lighter on them than the hamza. And the pattern mufay'il does not come outside of diminutive forms, except in three words: "musaytir", "mubaytir", and "muhaymin". We have mentioned in surah [al-Tur: 37], from Abu Ubaydah, that they are five words.

The third: the one who confirms what He informs, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that He is the Watcher over a thing and its Guardian, said by al-Khalil. Al-Khattabi said: some people of language said: al-haymanah is standing over a thing, and caring for it. And he recited:

Surely the best of people after their Prophet is his muhaymin, the one who recites, in what is known and what is denied.

He means the one who stands over the people after him with care for them. We have expanded on this explanation in [al-Ma'idah: 48], and we clarified the meaning of "al-Aziz" in [al-Baqarah: 129].

As for "al-Jabbar", there are four sayings concerning it.

The first: that He is the Great, said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that He is the one who overpowers people and compels them to what He wills, said by al-Qurazi and al-Suddi. Qatadah said: compelling His creation to what He wills. Al-Khattabi related: that He is the one who compels creation to what He wills of His command and prohibition. It is said: the sultan compelled him (jabarahu), and forced him (ajbarahu).

The third: that He is the one who mends the needs of creation and suffices them the means of livelihood and provision.

The fourth: that He is the one exalted above His creation, from their saying: the plant became jabbar when it grew tall and rose high. Al-Khattabi mentioned both meanings.

As for "al-Mutakabbir", there are five sayings concerning it.

The first: that He is the one who is exalted above every evil, said by Qatadah.

The second: that He is the one who is exalted above injustice to His servants, said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-228) The third: that He is the possessor of greatness (al-kibriya'), and this is the King, said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: that He is the one transcendent above the attributes of creation.

The fifth: that He is the one who exalts Himself over the most rebellious of His creatures when they contend with Him for greatness, so He breaks them. Al-Khattabi mentioned both of these. He said: the ta' in "al-Mutakabbir" is the ta' of singularity and exclusivity, because striving, affectation, and pride are not fitting for any of the created beings; rather, the mark of the servant is submission and humility. It has been said: al-Mutakabbir is from al-kibriya', which is the greatness of Allah, not from the kibr which is blameworthy in creation.

As for "al-Khaliq" (the Creator), al-Khattabi said: He is the one who initiates creation and brings it into being without a prior pattern. As for the descriptions of the children of Adam, the meaning of khalq is like the saying of Zuhayr:

And you indeed cut what you create, while others create and do not cut, meaning they wish for what they cannot reach.

He says: when you decide upon a thing you cut it, while others decide what they cannot cut through. "Al-Bari'" is the Creator; it is said: Allah created (bara'a) the creation, He creates them (yabra'uhum). "Al-Musawwir" (the Fashioner) is the one who brought His creation into being in various forms so that they may know one another by them. The meaning of taswir is outlining and shaping. Al-Hasan, Abu al-Jawza', Abu 'Imran, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "al-Bari' al-Musawwar" with a fatha on both the waw and the ra', meaning Adam, peace be upon him. What follows this has already been explained [al-A'raf: 180, and al-Isra': 110] to the end of the surah.
